sections.title: Why risk management matters
content: Risk management is a business decision, not just a technical one
Today: key terms, the loss formulas, the heat map, the four responses
The formulas are tested: expect at least one calculation
examples: A board asks: is a £3k-a-year control worth buying? The numbers answer it.
say: Every organisation has more threats than money to deal with them, so risk management is really about choosing where to spend.

The exam loves this topic because it mixes plain definitions with a bit of arithmetic. The sums are easy once you know which number goes where, and by the end you will be able to do them in your head.

checks.question: In your own words, why can an organisation not simply fix every security problem it finds?
checks.expect: Money, time and people are limited, so it has to prioritise by how likely and how damaging each problem is.

sections.title: What risk is: inherent and residual
content: Risk: the likelihood a threat exploits a weakness and causes harm
Often written as Threat x Vulnerability x Impact
Inherent risk: the level BEFORE any controls
Residual risk: what is LEFT AFTER controls, never zero
examples: Unpatched web server facing the internet: high inherent. Patch it and add a WAF: lower residual, but a zero-day could still land.
say: Three ingredients have to line up for there to be risk: someone or something that could cause harm, a weak spot it can use, and real damage if it succeeds. Take any one ingredient away and the risk shrinks.
Inherent is the raw starting point, before you have done anything. Residual is what you are still carrying once your controls are in place.
No control is perfect, so the leftover never reaches nothing. If an exam option claims controls brought it down to zero, that option is wrong.

misconceptions.belief: If we put enough controls in place, we can get the leftover danger down to nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Residual risk is always above zero; the aim is to bring it down to a level the organisation is willing to live with.

checks.question: A company installs a firewall in front of a database. Is the level that remains after installing it inherent or residual?
checks.expect: Residual, because it is what is left after a control has been applied.

sections.title: The loss formulas: SLE and ALE
content: SLE = AV x EF: the cost of ONE incident
ALE = SLE x ARO: the expected cost PER YEAR
EF is the percentage of the asset lost; ARO is how often per year
Decision rule: if a control costs less per year than the ALE, buy it
examples: £100k server, fire destroys 50%: SLE = £50k. Fire once a decade (ARO 0.1): ALE = £5k a year.
A fire suppression control costing £3k a year against a £5k ALE is worth it.
say: Start with one bad day. Take what the asset is worth, multiply by the share of it you would lose, and that is the single loss expectancy.
Then spread it across time. Multiply that one-off loss by how many times a year you expect it to happen. Once every ten years is nought point one, so the yearly figure is a tenth of the single loss.
The yearly figure is what you compare a control against. If protection costs less each year than the loss you expect each year, it pays for itself.

misconceptions.belief: The annualised rate of occurrence has to be a whole number, like once or twice.
misconceptions.correction: It can be a fraction: once every ten years is 0.1, once every four years is 0.25.

checks.question: A laptop worth two thousand pounds would be a total loss if stolen, and you expect one theft every two years. What is the yearly expected loss?
checks.expect: One thousand pounds: single loss of two thousand multiplied by a rate of 0.5.

checks.question: Which figure tells you the cost of one incident, and which tells you the cost per year?
checks.expect: Single loss expectancy is one incident; annual loss expectancy is per year.

sections.title: Qualitative versus quantitative, and the heat map
content: Quantitative: money values, objective, needs data, gives SLE and ALE
Qualitative: High, Medium, Low ratings, fast but subjective
Heat map: likelihood on one axis, impact on the other
High likelihood + high impact: treat urgently. Low + low: accept. Mixed: monitor
examples: A start-up with no incident history rates phishing as High likelihood, Medium impact and plots it on a heat map: qualitative.
say: There are two ways to size up a risk. One puts pounds on it, which is precise but only as good as your data. The other uses ratings, which is quick but depends on someone's judgement.
A heat map is what the ratings approach produces. Picture a grid: the top right corner, very likely and very damaging, is where you act first, and the bottom left can usually be accepted.

misconceptions.belief: Qualitative assessment is useless because it does not produce numbers.
misconceptions.correction: It is fast and useful when there is no reliable data; it just relies on judgement, so it is more subjective.

checks.question: If an exam question mentions exposure factor and pounds, which kind of assessment is it describing?
checks.expect: Quantitative, because it uses money values and formulas.

sections.title: The four ways to respond
content: Avoid: don't do the thing at all, e.g. don't launch the feature
Transfer: move the money impact elsewhere, e.g. cyber insurance
Mitigate: reduce likelihood or impact with controls or patching. The most common
Accept: formally document and sign off. For low risks, or when the fix costs more than the loss
examples: A firm buys cyber insurance. After a breach the insurer pays out, but customers' data is still exposed and the reputation damage is still the firm's.
say: Think of the four options as walk away, hand the bill to someone else, shrink it, or knowingly live with it.
Insurance is the trap here. It only moves the cost. The breach can still happen and you still suffer the disruption, so the risk itself has not gone anywhere.
Accepting is a deliberate, written decision with someone senior signing it. Simply ignoring a problem is not acceptance.

misconceptions.belief: Buying cyber insurance means the company no longer carries that risk.
misconceptions.correction: Insurance moves the money impact only; the event can still happen and the company still lives with the disruption.

checks.question: A team installs patches and adds multi-factor login to cut the chance of a break-in. Which of the four options is that?
checks.expect: Mitigate, because controls are reducing likelihood or impact.

sections.title: Risk vocabulary
content: Risk appetite: how much the organisation is WILLING to take on, set by the board
Risk tolerance: the acceptable variation around that appetite
Risk register: central record, every entry needs a NAMED OWNER
KRI (key risk indicator): a metric warning that a risk is rising
BIA (business impact analysis): which functions are critical and the impact if down. Drives RTO and RPO
examples: A rising number of unpatched servers each month is a key risk indicator.
The business impact analysis finds payroll can be down for 24 hours at most, which sets its recovery time objective.
say: Appetite is the overall stance the board sets. Tolerance is the wiggle room either side of it, how far you can drift before someone has to act.
A register is only useful if every line has a named person accountable for it. An entry owned by everyone is owned by no one.
A business impact analysis asks which processes the company cannot live without and what happens if they stop. Its answers feed the recovery time and recovery point objectives.

checks.question: What must every entry in a risk register have, and why?
checks.expect: A named owner, so someone is accountable for tracking and treating it.

checks.question: How is risk tolerance different from risk appetite?
checks.expect: Appetite is how much the organisation is willing to take on overall; tolerance is the acceptable variation around that level.

sections.title: Putting the numbers to work
content: Work out the single loss first, then the yearly figure
Compare the yearly figure with the yearly cost of the control
Then pick one of the four responses
say: Take this one slowly and say your working out loud. The sums are simple; the marks come from putting each number in the right place.
Once you have the yearly figure, the decision almost makes itself.

checks.question: If the exposure factor were 100 percent, what would the single loss equal?

application.scenario: A shop's customer database is valued at £80,000. A ransomware attack would make 50% of it unrecoverable. The shop expects such an attack once every four years. A backup service that would prevent most of the loss costs £6,000 a year.
application.question: Work out the single loss and the yearly expected loss, then tell me whether the backup service is worth buying and which of the four responses it represents.
application.expect: Single loss is 40,000 pounds; rate is 0.25, so the yearly loss is 10,000 pounds. The service costs 6,000 a year, less than 10,000, so buy it. That is mitigation.

sections.title: Key distinctions and traps
content: SLE = AV x EF (one incident). ALE = SLE x ARO (per year)
Inherent = before controls. Residual = after, never zero
Transfer moves the money impact only; the risk itself remains
Accept must be documented and signed off; ignoring is not accepting
Appetite set by the board; tolerance is the variation around it
examples: Control cheaper per year than the ALE: buy it.
say: If you remember one thing, make it the order of the sums: one incident first, then multiply by how often per year.
The classic traps are insurance making the risk vanish, accepting by doing nothing, and residual risk reaching zero. All three are wrong.

checks.question: Which response would you choose for a low-rated issue where the fix would cost more than the loss, and what must happen for it to count?
checks.expect: Accept, and it must be formally documented and signed off.

retrieval.question: Before we start, what do you think the word risk means in a security setting?
retrieval.expect: The chance that something bad happens, combined with how much harm it would do.

retrieval.question: Can you name any ways an organisation might deal with a danger other than fixing it?
retrieval.expect: Any of: avoiding it, insuring against it, or accepting it.

exam_questions.q: Which risk response stops the risky activity entirely?
exam_questions.why: Avoidance removes the danger by not doing the thing that creates it at all, for example not launching a feature.

exam_questions.q: Which response shifts some financial consequence to another party?
exam_questions.why: Transfer, such as buying cyber insurance, moves the money impact to someone else, although the underlying danger still remains.

exam_questions.q: What is the difference between risk and a vulnerability?
options: Risk combines likelihood and impact; a vulnerability is a weakness
A vulnerability is always an incident
exam_questions.answer: Risk combines likelihood and impact; a vulnerability is a weakness
exam_questions.why: A vulnerability is just a weak spot; risk is the chance a threat uses that weak spot multiplied by how much harm would follow.

added_facts: Heat map quadrants untangled from garbled text: high likelihood and high impact treat urgently, low and low accept, the two mixed corners monitor.
ARO can be a fraction (once every four years = 0.25); EF is a percentage of asset value lost.
Expanded RTO and RPO as recovery time objective and recovery point objective.
